554.title: The thread of compassion
554.hook: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot and truth the twist (Asa di Var, ang 471)
554.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the janamsakhi story of young Nanak and the sacred thread, and hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var as a call to wear the inner thread of compassion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vaariaa: the Guru's ointment on the eyes, the same world seen truly. Today, a turning point from Guru Nanak's own childhood, and the salok the tradition ties to it.

The courtyard is full. Relatives have come from nearby villages, food is cooking, and the family priest has arrived for an important day: a boy's investiture with the sacred thread. The boy is Nanak, still young, in Talwandi. The janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak written down generations later, tell what happened next. As the priest prepared the thread, the boy asked: what is this thread for? Will it last? Then he described the thread he would actually wear, and it wasn't made of cotton at all.
screen: `A COURTYARD FULL OF RELATIVES.` → `THE BOY NANAK AND THE THREAD.` → `A THREAD NOT MADE OF COTTON.`

segments.voice: The janeu is a sacred thread that Hindu families in some communities give their sons in a coming-of-age ceremony, worn across the body from the shoulder. For the families who keep it, it marks a second birth into learning and duty, and it's held with real reverence. The salok on ang 471, which Sikh tradition links to young Nanak's day, doesn't mock the thread. It asks for a deeper one. In paraphrase: make compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, and truth the twist. This is the sacred thread of the soul. If you have it, priest, then put it on me. Daiaa, compassion, is the raw cotton, the stuff everything else is spun from. Santokh, contentment, from the servants' pauri, is the thread itself, the long continuous strand. Jat, restraint, self-control, is the knot that holds it together. And sat, truth, is the twist that gives a thread its strength. Untwisted fiber pulls apart in the hands; spinners know it. Truth is what makes the whole thing hold. Notice the order. Compassion comes first, as the material; everything after is shaping it. A person could carry contentment, restraint, even truth, but without compassion there's nothing to spin. Sikhs remember this story as an early sign of who Nanak would become: not someone who rejects people's rituals for the sake of it, but someone always asking what's inside them. Tomorrow, what he said such a thread could survive.
screen: `THE JANEU: A SACRED THREAD.` · `COMPASSION, THE COTTON.` · `CONTENTMENT, RESTRAINT, TRUTH.` · `TRUTH IS THE TWIST THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION IS THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Hold a piece of string, or just your fingers, and touch it: compassion, the cotton; run along it: contentment, the thread. Tie a loose knot, restraint, and give it a gentle twist, truth. If you pray, say Waheguru as you hold it.
Janeu. The sacred thread. In Guru Nanak's salok, a thread of the soul: compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, restraint the knot, truth the twist.
Your line: compassion is the thread. Everything else is spun from it. Day five hundred fifty-four, done.

screen: `DAY 554 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE THREAD THAT WON'T BREAK.`

555.title: The thread that won't break
555.hook: such a thread doesn't break, burn, get dirty or wear out (Asa di Var, ang 471)
555.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that virtues and the praise of the One are what go with a person beyond death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janeu: compassion the cotton, the thread of the soul. Today, the second half of that salok, and four things that thread can survive.

Open any drawer at home and you'll find something that wore out. A sweater with elbows gone thin. A phone cable split near the plug. A favorite shirt washed one too many times. Everything made of fiber frays eventually. Cotton breaks under strain. It burns in a second near a flame. It picks up stains. And even protected from all that, time thins it out. Guru Nanak named all four ways a thread can fail, one by one, about the thread of compassion from yesterday.
screen: `A SWEATER WITH THIN ELBOWS.` → `EVERY FIBER FRAYS.` → `FOUR WAYS A THREAD FAILS.`

segments.voice: Here's how the salok on ang 471 continues, in paraphrase. Such a thread doesn't break. It doesn't get dirty. It doesn't burn. It isn't lost. Blessed, Nanak says, are the people who go about wearing it around their necks. Four nots. One way to hear them: breaking is strain, the hard week, the argument, the shock. Dirt is the slow grime of daily life: resentment, envy, gossip. Burning is the sudden fire: rage, disaster, loss. And being lost is time itself, the way things simply slip away. A cotton thread can't survive any of these for long. A thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth, the salok says, survives all four. Then Guru Nanak looks at the outer thread with plain eyes. It's bought for a few coins, he says, and put on in a ceremony. When the body dies, it falls away; the person leaves without it. Whatever is tied to the body goes the way of the body. The next salok in the var adds an answer. Through trust in the Name, honor arises, and praise of the One is the true thread. Worn that way, it doesn't break in the Court of the Lord. Sikh teaching reads this as a question about what goes with us. Not possessions, not status, not even the symbols we're given. What goes is what we've become. A grandmother who has worn that thread for decades, patient at the stove, honest at the market, takes it with her. The cotton one stays behind.
screen: `IT WON'T BREAK, STAIN, BURN, OR BE LOST.` · `THE OUTER THREAD FALLS AWAY.` · `PRAISE IS THE TRUE THREAD.` · `WHAT GOES IS WHAT WE'VE BECOME.` · then, large: `IT WON'T WEAR OUT.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself many years from now, most of today's worries long gone, and ask what in you will still be there: not a job title, maybe a way of listening, a patience, a love for certain people. Let one quality come forward, and picture it as a thread, already strong, getting stronger. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Compassion, one strand of the soul's thread: in Guru Nanak's salok, spun with contentment, restraint and truth, it doesn't break, get dirty, burn, or get lost, and it goes with you.
Your line: it won't wear out. What goes with us is what we've become. Five hundred fifty-five days now.

556.title: The impurity of greed
556.hook: the impurity of the mind is greed, of the tongue lying (Asa di Var, ang 472)
556.howItsDone: Sikh practice keeps no period of ritual impurity after a birth or death; the Sikh Rehat Maryada sets such observances aside, and Sikhs hear these saloks in the dawn singing of Asa di Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion: the soul's thread that won't wear out. Today Guru Nanak looks inside an old idea of being unclean.

Clean and dirty go deeper than germs. Shoes off at the door. Hands washed before eating. A kitchen counter nobody puts a bag on. Families and cultures draw those lines in different places, and they matter. In Guru Nanak's world, there was a strong idea called sootak: a time of ritual impurity that fell on a household after a birth or a death. For a set period, the family was considered unclean, and others might avoid their food. Guru Nanak took that word and asked where impurity really lives.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `SOOTAK: IMPURITY AFTER BIRTH OR DEATH.` → `WHERE DOES IMPURITY LIVE?`

segments.voice: The saloks are on ang 472, a short run of them. The first starts with a practical puzzle. If you believe in sootak, it says, in paraphrase, then sootak is everywhere. There are tiny creatures in cow dung and in firewood. Not a single grain of food is without life. Water itself gives life to everything. So how can anyone keep sootak out? It's already in the kitchen. Then the answer: Nanak, sootak isn't removed that way. Only spiritual wisdom washes it off. The next salok moves the word somewhere new. In paraphrase again: the sootak of the mind is greed. The sootak of the tongue is lying. Tomorrow, the eyes and the ears. For today, stay with those two. Lobh, greed, is the mind's impurity: the restless wanting that never says enough. Koorh, the word from the salok of the false king, is the tongue's. A household can follow every rule after a birth and still have a greedy mind at the table. A person can scrub their hands and still lie with their mouth. Guru Nanak isn't saying cleanliness doesn't matter; Sikh discipline includes bathing before the dawn prayers, and langar kitchens are kept clean. He's saying the impurity that really keeps people from the One isn't on the skin. A third salok finishes the thought: all sootak is doubt, attachment to something second. Birth and death come by the hukam, the divine order. They're not dirt. Greed and lying are.
screen: `SOOTAK: AN OLD IDEA OF IMPURITY.` · `LIFE IS IN EVERY GRAIN.` · `THE MIND'S IMPURITY: GREED.` · `THE TONGUE'S IMPURITY: LYING.` · then, large: `CLEAN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Rest your attention on your mouth for a moment, the tongue, the lips, the breath passing through. Think of where a small untruth tends to slip out, an excuse, an exaggeration, a shaded story, and let the tongue rest, quiet and plain. If you pray, say Waheguru with that clean tongue.
Sootak. Ritual impurity, once thought to fall on a home after a birth or death. Guru Nanak moves it inside: the mind's sootak is greed, the tongue's is lying.
Your line: clean tongue. The impurity that matters isn't on the skin. That's day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: Eyes and ears
557.hook: the impurity of the eyes is coveting, of the ears is gossip (Asa di Var, ang 472)
557.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of the four impurities in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching counts avoiding slander and coveting as part of daily discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sootak: the mind's impurity is greed, the tongue's is lying. Today the salok goes on to the eyes and the ears.

Scroll for ten minutes and count what comes in. Someone's new kitchen. Someone's vacation. A car you can't afford. A rumor about a person you've never met, and three hundred comments about it. None of it touched your hands. You didn't say a word. And yet the phone goes down with something new in it: a small want for what's theirs, a small taste for the rumor. Long before any feed, Guru Nanak named the two doors those come in through.
screen: `TEN MINUTES OF SCROLLING.` → `A SMALL WANT, A SMALL TASTE FOR RUMOR.` → `TWO DOORS IT CAME IN THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of the salok on ang 472, in paraphrase. The sootak of the eyes is looking with desire at another's spouse, another's wealth, another's beauty. The sootak of the ears is taking in slander, feeding on gossip. And the last line: Nanak, even those who seem like swans, pure and bright, are bound and led away, if they carry these. Look how exact this is. The eyes aren't impure for seeing. They're impure for a certain kind of looking: the look that wants what belongs to someone else. Coveting. It's quiet. Nobody else can see it. But it changes the one doing it, because every look that wants another's life makes your own life look smaller. The ears aren't impure for hearing, either. Gurbani is meant to be heard, sung aloud as kirtan. The impurity is in what the ears are fed. The salok's word for it is laaitbaaree: talebearing, backbiting, the tale carried about someone who isn't there. The salok pictures the ears almost eating it. And gossip, like coveting, doesn't need you to do anything. You only have to listen, and enjoy it a little. Put yesterday and today together and you have four doors: mind, tongue, eyes, ears. Greed, lies, coveting, gossip. Guru Nanak's point across all of it is the same. Washing the outside is easy. Keeping these four doors clean is the real purity, and it happens many times a day, in moments nobody else will ever see.
screen: `THE EYES: COVETING.` · `THE EARS: FEEDING ON GOSSIP.` · `IT CHANGES THE ONE WHO DOES IT.` · `FOUR DOORS: MIND, TONGUE, EYES, EARS.` · then, large: `CLEAN EYES, CLEAN EARS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something simple, a wall, a cup, the sky, and just see it, without wanting or judging. Then close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you, just hearing them, without a story. If you pray, let Waheguru be the one word you listen to inside.
Laaitbaaree, talebearing or backbiting: in Guru Nanak's salok, the eyes' impurity is coveting what is another's; the ears' impurity, laaitbaaree, is feeding on gossip.
Your line: clean eyes, clean ears. Four doors, kept clean in moments nobody sees. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

558.title: Speak sweetly
558.hook: speak insipid words and body and mind grow insipid (Asa di Var, ang 473)
558.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok on fikka speech in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and sweet, humble speech is counted among the marks of a Sikh's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday, laaitbaaree: clean eyes, clean ears, no feeding on gossip. Today the var comes back to the tongue, by way of the kitchen.

Taste a spoonful of dal before the salt goes in. It isn't bad, exactly. It isn't poisoned or burned. It's just flat. Lifeless. You take one bite and push the bowl away. Punjabi has a word for that taste: fikka. Tea without sugar is fikka. A party where nobody talks is fikka. And Guru Nanak used the same kitchen word, in a salok of the Asa di Var, for a kind of speech. Not lying, which we met two days ago. Something more ordinary, and maybe more common.
screen: `DAL BEFORE THE SALT.` → `FIKKA: FLAT, TASTELESS.` → `A KITCHEN WORD FOR SPEECH.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 473. In paraphrase: speaking fikka words, the body and mind become fikka. The fikka person is called fikka; the fikka person gets a fikka name. The fikka are cast out of the Court of the Lord, and have their faces spat upon. The fikka are called fools, and are punished with shoes. The word repeats until you can taste it. Fikka here means insipid, but it leans toward harsh, rude, sour: words with no sweetness and no care in them. A curt reply. A sarcastic dig. A cold one-word answer to someone who needed more. Here's the turn. The salok doesn't only say fikka words hurt the listener. It says they make the speaker fikka, body and mind. Speak flat and sour long enough, and you become flat and sour. Your reputation follows: people start to call you that. Anyone who's watched a person harden over the years has seen it happen. Words aren't just output. They're practice. Every sentence trains the one who says it. This connects back to mitthat neevee from day five hundred fifty-one: sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue. That was about who you are. Today is about how you get there. Sweet speech isn't flattery or fake niceness. It means words with some care cooked into them. Salt in the dal. Sugar in the tea. Something that makes the other person want to stay at the table.

Your line: sweet words, sweet life. Every sentence trains the one who says it. See you tomorrow.

559.title: The servant who argues
559.hook: a servant who serves while arguing proudly loses the master's favor (Asa di Var M2, ang 474)
559.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on the arguing servant in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh seva is meant to be done humbly, without complaint or display.

segments.voice: Yesterday, speak sweetly: fikka words make a fikka person, so care gets cooked into what we say. Today Guru Angad pictures someone who does the work, but can't stop talking back.

You ask someone at home to take out the trash. They do it. Eventually. But first there's a sigh, then a speech about how they always do everything, then a list of what you haven't done, then the bag dragged slowly to the door. The job is done. And somehow nobody in the house feels better. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short salok about exactly this: service with an argument attached.
screen: `THE TRASH, EVENTUALLY.` → `A SIGH, A SPEECH, A LIST.` → `THE JOB DONE, NOBODY BETTER.`

segments.voice: The salok is marked mahala 2, Guru Angad's, on ang 474. In paraphrase: a servant who works for a master, but serves with pride and argues, who talks a great deal, doesn't win the master's pleasure. One who loses the self and serves gains some honor. And the last line: Nanak, the one who clings to the Master meets the Master; that clinging is accepted. Notice what the arguing servant does right. He shows up. He does the work. The salok doesn't call him lazy. The problem is what he wraps around the work: gaarab, pride, and vaad, argument. Endless talk about how hard it is, how unfair, how much better he'd do it if he were in charge. The job gets done, but the service doesn't arrive, because service isn't only an action. It's a way of offering it. On day five hundred forty-five, in Guru Nanak's pauri, the contented servants served and were accepted. This salok, his successor's, shows the shadow side of the same picture: the proud served too, and argued, and lost the favor. Sikhs tell a story about Guru Angad himself, when he was still called Bhai Lehna. Guru Nanak asked for hard and dirty jobs to be done, and while others objected, Lehna simply did them. Tradition holds that's part of why Guru Nanak chose him. Whatever the details, the salok reads like it came from someone who had lived it: serving without the speech.
screen: `PRIDE AND ARGUMENT AROUND THE WORK.` · `THE JOB DONE, THE SERVICE NOT.` · `LOSE THE SELF, GAIN HONOR.` · `BHAI LEHNA SIMPLY DID IT.` · then, large: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Think of one task waiting for you that you'd normally do with a sigh: a chore, an errand, a request from someone. Picture doing it all the way through with no commentary, no list, no speech in your head, just the work, offered; if something in you resists, let it, and breathe. 560.title: How each pauri sums up

segments.voice: Yesterday, gaarab, pride, and your line: serve without argument. That closes a week: the thread of compassion, sootak, laaitbaaree, sweet speech, gaarab. Today, how the var holds them all together.
screen: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.` · `A WEEK: THREADS, PURITY, SPEECH, SERVICE.`

segments.voice: Climb the steps down to the water at a gurdwara sarovar, or a staircase in an old Punjabi house, and every step has a name: pauri. The same word means a ladder rung. It's also the name of the stanzas you've been hearing for weeks without quite noticing them. Japji is built of pauris. So is every var in the Guru Granth Sahib. For three weeks we've mostly listened to saloks, the short verses about trees, threads and scales. Today, the steps they sit on.
screen: `A STEP DOWN TO THE WATER.` → `PAURI: A STEP, A RUNG.` → `THE STEPS UNDER THE SALOKS.`

segments.voice: A var, as we heard on day five hundred thirty-six, is an old Punjabi ballad form, sung about heroes and battles. Its stanzas are pauris, and in a var they march: each one a step forward in the story. The Guru Granth Sahib has twenty-two vars. In the Asa di Var, the pauris are Guru Nanak's, twenty-four of them, and they carry the main line of the poem: who the One is, how creation stands, what a true servant is like, what the Guru does. In front of each pauri sit two or more saloks, some Guru Nanak's, some Guru Angad's. Many scholars hold that they were set beside the pauris when Guru Arjan compiled the Granth, gathered by theme to open up the step that follows. So the saloks wander: a silk-cotton tree, a cartload of books, a thread, a kitchen. They make you see something. Then the pauri arrives and gathers what you've seen into one step forward. You've felt this already. The pauri where Guru Nanak says he's a sacrifice to the True Guru, who put wisdom on his eyes, came after saloks about show without substance. The saloks showed the problem; the pauri named the turning. Hear the Asa di Var sung and you can feel the rhythm: wander, gather; wander, gather. Many small pictures, then one step up. It's a way of learning that doesn't rush. You don't climb the whole staircase at once. You take the next pauri.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD OF HEROES.` · `24 PAURIS, GURU NANAK'S.` · `SALOKS WANDER, THE PAURI GATHERS.` · `WANDER, GATHER; ONE STEP UP.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka or an app with the Asa di Var, read one pauri slowly, all the way through, in Gurmukhi or in translation. If not, hold the pauri from this week in mind: the contented ones served, did good, ate little, broke the world's chains, and the One kept giving more; let it sit as one step, complete, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.
Pauri. A step, a ladder rung, and a stanza. In the Asa di Var, each of Guru Nanak's twenty-four pauris gathers the saloks before it into one step forward.
Your line: step by step. Nobody climbs a whole staircase in one stride. See you tomorrow.
